title: Five loaves and two fish (John 6:1–14)
hook: a boy hands over his lunch and five thousand are fed
carry: what you hand over is enough

segments.voice: Last week ended with the workers hired late, and the line grace isn't a wage. Were you glad for someone's gift? Day fifty. A new week: signs on the road. And it starts with a lunch.
screen: `GRACE ISN'T A WAGE.` → `WEEK EIGHT: SIGNS ON THE ROAD.`

segments.voice: A hillside by the Sea of Galilee, near Passover, green with spring grass. A huge crowd has followed Jesus out here, thousands of people, a long way from any town. It's getting late. Everybody's hungry. Jesus turns to Philip, one of his disciples, and asks, in the Douay-Rheims: "Whence shall we buy bread, that these may eat?" John adds that he asked this to test him, because he already knew what he would do. Philip does the math and panics. Two hundred days' wages wouldn't buy enough for each of them to get a little. You know the feeling: the need is enormous, and what you've got is nothing. Today: a boy, and his lunch.
screen: `A HILLSIDE, A HUGE CROWD.` → `WHERE WILL WE BUY BREAD?` → `PHILIP DOES THE MATH.`

segments.voice: Then Andrew speaks up, and his sentence is honest and a little embarrassed: "There is a boy here that hath five barley loaves, and two fishes; but what are these among so many?" Only John tells us it was a boy. And only John tells us the loaves were barley. Barley bread was the cheap bread, what poor families ate. This is a kid's packed lunch, and not a fancy one. Jesus says: make the people sit down. There's a lot of grass there, John notes, and about five thousand men sit down, not counting women and children. Then Jesus takes the loaves, and gives thanks, and hands them out, and the fish too, as much as anyone wants. The Greek word for gave thanks is the root of a word Catholics know well: Eucharist. That's not an accident. John's chapter six goes on, the next day, to Jesus calling himself the bread of life, and the Church has always read this hillside meal as pointing toward the Mass. Then a detail that's easy to miss. When everyone's full, Jesus says: "Gather up the fragments that remain, lest they be lost." They fill twelve baskets with leftovers. Nothing wasted. More left over than they started with. This is the only miracle, apart from the resurrection, that all four Gospels tell. And in John's telling, it starts with a child who handed over what he had, even though everyone could see it wasn't enough.
screen: `FIVE BARLEY LOAVES, TWO FISH.` · `A BOY'S CHEAP LUNCH.` · `HE GAVE THANKS — EUCHARIST.` · `TWELVE BASKETS LEFT OVER.` · then, large: `BUT WHAT ARE THESE AMONG SO MANY?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Settle and breathe. Think of a need that seems too big: a friend's grief, a neighbor's struggle, a cause you care about. And think of what you actually have. Not much. Ten minutes. Twenty dollars. One skill. A listening ear. Five loaves and two fish. Choose one small thing you think won't matter, and picture handing it over anyway. If you pray, you can offer it to God and let him do the math. The bell holds the time.
Five loaves and two fish. A boy's lunch, handed over, and a hillside of thousands fed, with baskets to spare. Today's word.
screen: `FIVE LOAVES AND TWO FISH — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: what you hand over is enough. Today, give the small thing you think won't matter. Day fifty.

howItsDone: Catholics read John 6 over several summer Sundays in the year of Mark, from the feeding on the hillside through the bread of life discourse, and hear it as pointing to the Eucharist.

fork.setup: you're Andrew. thousands of hungry people, and all you've found is a boy with five loaves and two fish. what do you do?
options: bring it to Jesus, even though it isn't enough.
tell everyone to go home and find their own food.
fork.reveal: he brings it: “but what are these among so many?” Jesus gives thanks, and five thousand eat, with twelve baskets left.

original.note: Greek: having given thanks. The root of the word Eucharist.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus makes food appear for a crowd.
what it means: a boy hands over a poor lunch, Jesus gives thanks, and there's more than enough, with nothing wasted.
what a scholar hears: eucharistēsas, having given thanks. John 6 moves on to the bread of life, and the Church reads it toward the Mass.

notes: Douay-Rheims wording of John 6:5, 6:9, 6:12 given from memory; confirm.
'Not counting women and children' comes from Matthew 14:21, not John; the script folds it in. Confirm or remove.
Two hundred denarii (6:7) rendered as 'two hundred days' wages'; confirm.
Barley bread as the bread of the poor: standard background; confirm.
'The only miracle, apart from the resurrection, that all four Gospels tell': commonly stated; confirm.
John 6 read on Sundays 17–21 of Ordinary Time in Year B; confirm.
